definitions.definition: In BhG 4–6: the teaching the Lord calls 'this imperishable yoga', taught by him to Vivasvat, handed down through the royal sages, lost over time and renewed to Arjuna (4.1–3); what is called renunciation is yoga, since no one becomes a yogin without renouncing intention (6.2); defined as the disconnection from union with suffering (duḥkha-saṃyoga-viyoga) — the state in which the mind stilled by practice comes to rest and one sees the self by the self (6.20–23); to be practised with determination and an undespondent mind (6.23).

In BhG 5–6: renunciation of actions (karma-saṃnyāsa) and the yoga of action both bring the highest good, the latter being superior (5.2); the constant renunciant (nitya-saṃnyāsin) is the one who neither hates nor desires (5.3); renunciation is hard to attain without yoga (5.6); the self-controlled embodied one renounces all actions with the mind (5.13); the renunciant is the one who does the required action without depending on its fruit, not the one without sacred fire or rites (6.1); what is called renunciation is yoga (6.2). 4.41 speaks of actions renounced through yoga.

BhG 5.2: the yoga of action, which together with renunciation brings the highest good and is superior to the renunciation of action; in 5.10–12 it is acting with actions placed in Brahman, abandoning attachment and the fruit, for purification of the self.

BhG 4.16–18: action, about whose nature even the wise are bewildered; it must be understood together with vikarma and inaction, for the way of action is deep; the wise see inaction in action. All sacrifices are born of action (4.32); all action culminates in knowledge (4.33) and is burnt by the fire of knowledge (4.37); actions do not stain the Lord (4.14).

BhG 4.16–18: inaction, to be understood alongside action and vikarma; the wise see inaction in action and action in inaction; one who has abandoned attachment to the fruit does nothing though fully engaged in action (4.20).
BhG 4.17: one of the three things to be understood along with action and inaction; the verse does not define it (commentators: forbidden action, or action in its varied forms).

BhG 4.23–33: sacrifice as the frame of all action — the action of one who acts for sacrifice dissolves (4.23); Brahman is every element of the offering (4.24); the word is extended to offering the senses into restraint, breath into breath, material things, austerity, yoga, study and knowledge (4.25–30); those who eat the nectar-remainder of sacrifice go to Brahman, and not even this world belongs to the non-sacrificer (4.31); all sacrifices are born of action (4.32); the sacrifice of knowledge is best (4.33). Result-seekers sacrifice to the deities for quick success (4.12). The Lord is the enjoyer of sacrifices (5.29).
BhG 4.28, 4.33: the sacrifice of knowledge, offered by ascetics of strict vows; better than sacrifice made of material things, since all action without exception culminates in knowledge.

BhG 4.33–42 and 5.15–17: knowledge — learned from knowers who have seen the truth through prostration, questioning and service (4.34); by it one is not deluded again and sees all beings in the self and in the Lord (4.35); a raft across all wrong (4.36); a fire that burns all actions (4.37); the supreme purifier, found within oneself in time by one perfected in yoga (4.38); obtained by the faithful, intent and sense-restrained, and followed by supreme peace (4.39); it cuts doubt like a sword (4.42). It is covered by ignorance, which deludes creatures; where ignorance is destroyed, knowledge illumines the highest like the sun (5.15–16). 6.8 pairs it with realized knowledge (vijñāna).
BhG 4.19, 4.37: the fire of knowledge, which burns up actions — the learned one's actions are burnt in it, and as a kindled fire turns firewood to ash, it turns all actions to ash.
BhG 4.2: succession — the chain (Vivasvat, Manu, Ikṣvāku) through which the royal sages received and knew the yoga before it was lost.
BhG 4.2: the royal sages, who knew the yoga received by succession.

BhG 4.6: the Lord, though unborn, imperishable and lord of beings, comes into being by his own māyā (ātmamāyā), taking his stand on his own nature (commentators divide: power of appearance, or the Lord's knowledge/will).

BhG 4.6: the lord of beings, who is unborn yet comes into being; 5.29: the great lord of all worlds (sarvaloka-maheśvara), enjoyer of sacrifices and austerities and friend of all beings, knowing whom one attains peace.
BhG 4.6: the Lord's own nature (prakṛtiṃ svām), on which he takes his stand in coming into being.
BhG 4.7–8: dharma, whose decline together with the rise of adharma is the occasion of the Lord's coming into being, and whose firm establishment is one of its purposes, age after age.
BhG 4.7: adharma, whose rise, with the decline of dharma, occasions the Lord's sending himself forth.
BhG 4.8: 'age after age' (yuge yuge) — the Lord comes into being in successive ages to establish dharma.
BhG 4.13: the fourfold class order (cāturvarṇya), created by the Lord according to the division of qualities (guṇa) and actions (karma).
BhG 5.14: agency, which the master (prabhu) does not create for the world — nor actions, nor the link of action and fruit; nature (svabhāva) acts. Cf. the Lord as maker yet non-doer (akartṛ) in 4.13.
BhG 5.14: inherent nature, which is what acts (svabhāvas tu pravartate), rather than the master creating agency, actions or their fruit.
BhG 5.13: the embodied one, who, having renounced all actions with the mind, sits at ease in the city of nine gates, neither acting nor causing action.
BhG 6.3: the sage wishing to ascend to yoga, for whom action is said to be the means.

literal: one who has ascended to yoga

definitions.definition: BhG 6.3–4: one who has ascended to yoga — when one is attached neither to sense objects nor to actions and has renounced all intentions; for him calm (śama) is said to be the means.
BhG 6.3: calm, said to be the means for one who has ascended to yoga (as action is for one ascending).

BhG 4–6: the recurring title of one established in yoga — the one who sees inaction in action (4.18); who withstands the surge of desire and anger (5.23); the yogin satisfied with knowledge and realized knowledge, unmoved, to whom clod, stone and gold are the same (6.8); the one whose restrained mind rests in the self alone, free of craving (6.18). The same word means 'measured' in food, recreation, effort, sleep and waking (6.17). The one who worships the Lord with faith is the most yoked (yuktatama, 6.47); the unyoked (ayukta) is bound (5.12).

literal: standing on the peak / like an anvil

definitions.definition: BhG 6.8: said of the yoked yogin — one who stands unmoved.
BhG 6.8: realized knowledge, paired with knowledge (jñāna); the yoked yogin's self is satisfied with both.

BhG 5.18: the learned see the same in a learned and humble brāhmaṇa, a cow, an elephant, a dog and an outcaste; 6.29: the one yoked in yoga sees the same everywhere (sarvatra samadarśana), the self in all beings and all beings in the self.

In BhG 4–6 the idea appears as sāmya, 'sameness': those whose mind is established in sameness overcome creation here, for Brahman is flawless and the same (5.19); Arjuna calls the yoga taught 'sameness' (6.33). Also 'the same in success and failure' (4.22) and 'equal mind' (samabuddhi) toward friend and foe, good and wicked (6.9).

BhG 5.24–26: attained by the yogin who has happiness, delight and light within and has become Brahman; by seers whose stains are destroyed, doubts cut, self restrained and who delight in the welfare of all beings; it is present all around the ascetics free of desire and anger who know the self.
BhG 5.24, 6.27: said of the yogin who, having become Brahman, attains brahma-nirvāṇa (5.24) and to whom the highest happiness comes (6.27).
BhG 6.15: the peace which culminates in nirvāṇa (nirvāṇa-paramā) and abides in the Lord, attained by the yogin who always yokes himself; cf. brahma-nirvāṇa, 5.24–26.

BhG 4–6: supreme peace follows soon on obtaining knowledge (4.39); the yoked one who abandons the fruit attains the peace of steadfastness (5.12); knowing the Lord as enjoyer of sacrifices and friend of all beings brings peace (5.29); the peace culminating in nirvāṇa, abiding in the Lord (6.15).
BhG 5.17: the non-return reached by those whose intellect, self, steadiness and final goal are That, their stains shaken off by knowledge.

BhG 4–6: the one with faith, intent and sense-restrained obtains knowledge (4.39); the faithless perishes (4.40); the one endowed with faith who falls from yoga through insufficient striving is not lost (6.37–45); the faithful worshipper of the Lord is the most yoked (6.47).

BhG 4.40–42: doubt — the doubting self perishes and has neither this world nor the next nor happiness; doubt born of ignorance, lodged in the heart, is cut by knowledge (the sword of knowledge). 6.39: Arjuna asks the Lord, as the only one who can, to cut his doubt.
BhG 6.35: practice, by which, together with dispassion, the restless mind is held; 6.44: former practice (pūrvābhyāsa) carries the fallen yogin on in a new birth even without his will.
BhG 6.35: dispassion, by which, together with practice, the mind that is hard to restrain is held.

BhG 6.7: for one who has conquered the self and is at peace, the supreme self is composed (samāhita) amid cold and heat, pleasure and pain, honour and dishonour (the construal is disputed by commentators).
BhG 6.44: the 'word-Brahman' which even one who merely wishes to know yoga passes beyond (commentators: the Veda and the works it enjoins).

BhG 6.41: one fallen from yoga, who reaches the worlds of the meritorious, dwells there long, and is reborn among the pure and prosperous or in a family of wise yogins, where he regains his former understanding and strives again (6.37–45).

literal: likeness to oneself; analogy with oneself

definitions.definition: BhG 6.32: the highest yogin sees the same everywhere, pleasure or pain, by likeness to himself.
BhG 4.24: the offering (or instrument of offering) is Brahman, the oblation is Brahman, offered by Brahman into the fire that is Brahman; Brahman is reached by one absorbed in action as Brahman.

literal: one who has seen the truth

definitions.definition: BhG 4.34: the knowers who have seen the truth, who will teach knowledge to one who approaches them with prostration, questioning and service.
BhG 4.34: prostration, the first of the three ways (with questioning and service) of approaching the knowers of truth.
BhG 4.34: service, with prostration and questioning, by which knowledge is learned from the knowers of truth. 6.20 uses 'yoga-sevā' for the practice of yoga.

BhG 4.27–30, 5.27: the activities of prāṇa are offered into the fire of self-restraint (4.27); prāṇa is offered into apāna and apāna into prāṇa, and their movements restrained (4.29); those regulating food offer prāṇas into prāṇas (4.30); prāṇa and apāna moving within the nostrils are made equal (5.27).
BhG 4.29, 5.27: the breath paired with prāṇa — each is offered into the other and their movements restrained (4.29); both, moving within the nostrils, are made equal (5.27).
BhG 4.29: those devoted to breath-regulation restrain the movements of prāṇa and apāna, offering each into the other, as one of the sacrifices.
BhG 4.26–27: restraint — its fires receive the senses (4.26), and the yoga of self-restraint (ātma-saṃyama-yoga), kindled by knowledge, receives all activities of the senses and of breath (4.27).

notes: In the Gītā the word means restraint (of senses, mind), not the Yoga Sūtra's technical triad.

definitions.definition: BhG 4–6: austerity offered as sacrifice (tapo-yajña, 4.28); many purified by the austerity of knowledge came to the Lord's being (4.10); the Lord is enjoyer of sacrifices and austerities (5.29); the yogin is greater than the ascetics (tapasvin) (6.46).
BhG 4.28: study/recitation offered as sacrifice by ascetics of strict vows, together with knowledge.
BhG 5.15–16: ignorance, which covers knowledge and deludes creatures, and which is destroyed by knowledge of the self; 4.42: doubt is born of ignorance; 4.40: the ignorant (ajña) perishes.
BhG 4.35: knowing which one does not again fall into delusion; 5.15: creatures are deluded because knowledge is covered by ignorance; 5.20: the knower of Brahman is undeluded.

BhG 4–6: the learned one's undertakings are free of desire and intention (4.19); no one becomes a yogin without renouncing intention (6.2); the one who has ascended to yoga has renounced all intentions (6.4); desires arise from intention and are to be abandoned without remainder (6.24).

BhG 4–6: undertakings free of desire mark the learned (4.19); the unyoked is bound through the drive of desire (5.12); the surge of desire and anger is to be withstood before leaving the body (5.23); brahma-nirvāṇa is near those free of desire and anger (5.26); desires born of intention are to be abandoned in meditation (6.24); the yoked one is free of craving for all desires (6.18).

BhG 4–6: those free of passion, fear and anger came to the Lord's being (4.10); the surge of desire and anger is to be withstood (5.23); the ascetics free of desire and anger have brahma-nirvāṇa near (5.26); the sage from whom desire, fear and anger are gone is ever liberated (5.28).

BhG 4.22, 5.3: the one beyond the pairs of opposites is not bound though acting; free of them the constant renunciant is easily released; 6.7 lists such pairs: cold and heat, pleasure and pain, honour and dishonour.

BhG 4–5: the one who knows the Lord as unstained by action is not bound by actions (4.14); the one beyond the opposites is not bound though acting (4.22); the constant renunciant is easily released from bondage (5.3); the unyoked, attached to the fruit, is bound (5.12).

BhG 4.20, 5.12: having abandoned attachment to the fruit of action, one does nothing though engaged in action (4.20); the yoked one abandons the fruit and attains the peace of steadfastness (5.12); cf. 6.1 acting without depending on the fruit.

BhG 5–6: the happiness in the self, found by one unattached to external contacts, imperishable (5.21); enjoyments born of contact are sources of suffering (5.22); happiness, delight and light within (5.24); boundless happiness grasped by the intellect and beyond the senses (6.21); the highest happiness and the boundless happiness of contact with Brahman (6.27–28).

BhG 5–6: contact-born enjoyments are wombs of suffering (5.22); yoga, practised with moderation, destroys suffering (6.17); yoga is the disconnection from union with suffering, in which one is not shaken even by heavy sorrow (6.22–23).
BhG 4.15: the ancient seekers of liberation, who, knowing the Lord's freedom from action's stain, performed action.

BhG 5–6: the sage yoked in yoga reaches Brahman soon (5.6); the sage intent on liberation, restrained in senses, mind and intellect, is ever free (5.28); the sage wishing to ascend to yoga has action as the means (6.3).

BhG 4.28: ascetics of strict vows offer study and knowledge as sacrifice; 5.26: for ascetics free of desire and anger brahma-nirvāṇa is near; 6.37: the 'non-striver' (ayati) with faith who falls from yoga.
BhG 6.20: the mind stilled (niruddha) by the practice of yoga comes to rest; 6.34: Arjuna thinks restraining (nigraha) the mind as hard as restraining the wind.
BhG 6.12: seated on the seat, making the mind one-pointed, one should practise yoga for purification of the self.

BhG 6.24–35: the mind restrains the troop of senses (6.24) and is made to abide in the self (6.25); whenever the restless, unsteady mind wanders it is to be brought back (6.26); Arjuna calls it restless, turbulent, strong and obstinate, as hard to restrain as the wind (6.34); the Lord grants this and says it is held by practice and dispassion (6.35). 5.13: actions are renounced with the mind.

BhG 6.12–20: the activities of citta are restrained in meditation (6.12); when the restrained citta rests in the self alone one is 'yoked' (6.18); the yogin of restrained citta is like a lamp in a windless place (6.19); citta stilled by practice comes to rest (6.20).

BhG 5–6: yogins act with body, mind, intellect and senses (5.11); the knower of Brahman is steady in intellect (5.20); boundless happiness is grasped by the intellect (6.21); one comes to rest by the intellect held in steadfastness (6.25); the fallen yogin regains the connection with understanding of his former body (6.43).
BhG 6.25: the intellect held in steadfastness, by which one gradually comes to rest.
BhG 6.11–12: the seat set up in a clean place — firm, neither too high nor too low, covered with cloth, deerskin and kuśa grass — on which the yogin sits to practise.
BhG 6.14: the meditator is to be firm in the vow of the brahmacārin (brahmacāri-vrata).

BhG 4–6: Arjuna receives the secret yoga as the Lord's devotee (bhakta) and friend (4.3); the Lord receives people as they approach him (4.11); the yogin established in oneness worships (bhajati) the Lord in all beings (6.31); of all yogins the faithful one who worships (bhajate) him with inner self gone into him is the most yoked (6.47).

BhG 5.4–5: Sāṃkhya, which the childish, not the learned, call separate from Yoga; the place reached by the followers of Sāṃkhya is reached also by those of Yoga, and one who sees them as one sees. In context it stands with renunciation/knowledge.

BhG 4–6: Brahman is every element of the sacrificial act and the goal of one absorbed in action as Brahman (4.24); those who eat the remainder of sacrifice go to the eternal Brahman (4.31); the sage yoked in yoga reaches Brahman (5.6); actions are placed in Brahman (5.10); Brahman is flawless and the same, so the equal-minded are established in it (5.19); the knower of Brahman is established in Brahman (5.20); becoming Brahman, one attains brahma-nirvāṇa (5.24); contact with Brahman is boundless happiness (6.28).

BhG 4–6: the word ranges over self, mind and person: one should raise the self by the self, the self being its own friend or enemy (6.5–6); knowledge shows all beings in the self (4.35); the yoked one sees the self in all beings and all beings in the self (6.29); in the stilled mind one sees the self by the self and is content in the self (6.20); the happiness in the self (5.21).

BhG 4–6: the senses are offered into the fires of restraint (4.26); the knower holds that the senses move among the objects of the senses (5.9); the troop of senses is restrained by the mind in meditation (6.24); happiness in yoga lies beyond the senses (6.21).
